questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Composite pattern?

options.text: Compose objects into tree structures and let clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly
Decouple an abstraction from its implementation
Attach responsibilities to an object dynamically

questions.explanation: Composite is about part-whole trees with uniform treatment. Decoupling two dimensions = Bridge; adding responsibilities = Decorator; one instance = Singleton.

questions.prompt: Match each Composite role to its description.

pairs.right: The shared interface for all nodes
A node that holds children and delegates to them

questions.explanation: Leaves and composites share the Component interface; composites implement operations by delegating to their children.

questions.prompt: How does a composite typically implement an operation such as size()?

options.text: By recursing — delegating to each child and combining the results
By converting its interface to another
By storing a single global value

questions.explanation: A folder's size() sums the sizes of its children, each of which may itself be a folder — recursion through the tree.

questions.prompt: Composite represents ____-whole hierarchies, where wholes are made of parts that may themselves be wholes.
questions.explanation: The pattern models part-whole hierarchies such as files within folders within folders.

questions.prompt: What is the well-known design tension in Composite?

options.text: Whether add/remove belong on the shared Component (forcing leaves to implement them) or only on the Composite
Whether to use a private constructor

questions.explanation: Putting child-management on the Component forces leaves to implement methods that don't apply, often by throwing — a Liskov trade-off.

questions.prompt: When is Composite the WRONG choice?

options.text: When the data is a flat collection, not a genuine tree
When you have folders nested inside folders
When you want to treat leaves and groups uniformly
When a UI panel contains other panels

questions.explanation: Composite earns its keep only with real nesting; a flat list gains nothing from it.
